name: CABOT CORP

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That I have over-corrected, and the fiscal 2026 cash-flow collapse is a working-capital artifact I should have looked through rather than capitalised. Cabot itself publishes Discretionary Free Cash Flow precisely BECAUSE it strips the working-capital movement, and that figure - $225M over nine months - is holding up far better than free cash flow. The $44M of working capital consumed in the June quarter is inventory and receivables inflating with feedstock prices; when prices flatten it reverses, and a metals-and-chemicals converter that is growing its borrowing base is not a business in distress. On this reading the correct base is closer to the engine's $454.7M than to my $357M, the market's -4.9% is a real discount, and the +86.7% gap is at least partly genuine.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: The fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter and full-year cash flow statement (September year end, reported late October/November) showing whether the working-capital build reverses and full-year operating cash flow recovers toward the $595-692M range of fiscal 2023-2025, or settles near the ~$380M the nine-month run rate implies.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Some of it, and it genuinely moderated my answer - it is why I used the sustaining base of $357M rather than the $247M that fiscal 2026 total-capex free cash flow implies, and why this is no_edge rather than rich. What the counter cannot explain is the EARNINGS line, which working capital does not touch: adjusted EPS guidance of $6.15-6.45 is down about 12% year on year, and that is a margin fact, not a timing fact. Nor does it rescue the engine's base, because $454.7M is the mean of fiscal 2023-2025 - three years that ended before the decline began. Two defensible bases, $357M and $247M, put the required growth at +0.5% and +9.2%; the engine's number is outside that range entirely.
devils_advocate.unresolved: Whether Battery Materials has any near-term earnings materiality. Cabot describes brownfield expansion and capacity investment but I could not find a segment revenue or EBITDA disclosure for it in the Q3 release, so I cannot size the growth the $41M/year of growth capex is buying. That is the single input that would move the bull case, and I could not obtain it.

what_changed: Q3 fiscal 2026 (2026-08-03): adjusted EPS $1.67, up 4% sequentially, with Performance Chemicals offsetting Reinforcement Materials margin pressure. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance TIGHTENED to $6.15-6.45 from $6.00-6.50. Operating cash flow of $75M in the quarter absorbed $44M of working capital on rapidly rising raw-material costs. Net debt/EBITDA 1.4x, liquidity $1.3B, cash $250M. A $19M discrete tax charge on ceasing carbon black production at Campana, Argentina drove a 79% quarterly effective rate. 2026-08-12: priced $350M of 4.950% senior notes due 2029. 2026-09-15: Steve Delahunt appointed INTERIM CFO - this is not a governance red flag, it is the consequence of CEO Sean Keohane retiring after 25 years and CFO Erica McLaughlin being promoted to succeed him.
consensus_case: At $79.20 the market is paying roughly 9x a normalized unlevered cash flow for a carbon-black franchise in visible earnings decline. Cabot has just tightened fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $6.15-6.45, which is DOWN about 12% on fiscal 2025, and the decline is concentrated in Reinforcement Materials, where Chinese overcapacity and soft replacement-tyre demand cap pricing while feedstock costs rise faster than contract resets. The market's implied -4.9% is not pessimism about the enterprise, it is an assumption that the highest-margin segment shrinks and that Battery Materials - the growth story the sell-side likes - remains too small to offset it for several more years. Cabot is also absorbing a real cash-conversion problem: nine months of fiscal 2026 produced $278M of operating cash flow against $665M for the whole of fiscal 2025.
base_case_rationale: Cabot discloses sustaining and compliance capital expenditure SEPARATELY from total capex, which per the AROC rule means CFO-less-total-capex is the wrong definition of owner earnings here. Its own reconciliation for the nine months of fiscal 2026 reads: operating cash flow $278M, total capex $152M, of which sustaining and compliance capex is $111M - so roughly 27% of capital spending is capacity expansion, mostly Battery Materials brownfield. Discretionary free cash flow (CFO less sustaining capex less working-capital movement) was $225M over nine months, about $300M annualised, and adding back after-tax interest of roughly $57M gives a sustaining base near $357M. The pairing rule is absolute: a sustaining base takes near-zero growth, because the growth capex that would buy the growth has been excluded. I underwrite +1.5% - essentially inflation-linked pricing on a mature reinforcement franchise, with Performance Chemicals and Battery Materials contributing just enough to offset Reinforcement Materials' structural decline. That is materially below the naive +7.3% revenue CAGR baseline, which is measured off the 2020 trough and is mostly carbon-black price inflation rather than volume.
key_risks: Reinforcement Materials spread compression from Chinese carbon-black overcapacity and soft replacement-tyre demand
Working-capital absorption on rising feedstock costs may persist rather than reverse
Simultaneous CEO and CFO transition: Keohane retiring, McLaughlin promoted, an interim CFO in the seat from October
Battery Materials capex is being spent ahead of disclosed segment economics
Plant closures (Campana, Argentina) signal footprint rationalisation with associated discrete charges
watch_for: Fiscal 2026 full-year cash flow statement: does the working-capital build reverse, or is ~$380M of operating cash flow the new run rate
First disclosed Battery Materials segment revenue or EBITDA
Fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS guidance against the declining $6.15-6.45 fiscal 2026 range
